newsitem.title: CANADA: Canada's Hollinger bids for Southam majority.
newsitem.headline: Canada's Hollinger bids for Southam majority.

text.p: International publisher Hollinger Inc. Thursday ended months of speculation and made an offer for just enough shares in Southam Inc. to give it a majority stake in Canada's largest newspaper publisher.

Hollinger, which now holds 41 percent of Southam, on Thursday offered C$18.75 ($13.94) per share, or C$131 million ($97.38 million) in total, for 7 million shares of the company, enough to raise its stake to 50.1 percent.
But it reserved the option to buy more or less, depending on how many shares are deposited under the offer.

Canadian-born press baron Conrad Black's companies Hollinger and Hollinger International Inc. own or have interests in such well-known papers as the London Telegraph, the Chicago Sun-Times, the Jerusalem Post and the Sydney Morning Herald.

In May, he boosted his stake in Southam, which owns 20 dailies including the Montreal Gazette, the Ottawa Citizen and the Vancouver Sun, to 41 percent from below 20 percent by buying Power Corp. of Canada's 16.35 million Southam shares for C$18 ($13.38) a share.
The C$18.75 price is based upon the amount paid to Power "adjusted to reflect the time value of money," Hollinger said.
Black prefers to own more than 50 percent of those assets he buys so he can consolidate their earnings on his holding companies' balance sheets.
He has long said that he intended to raise his stake to a majority and may one day might make an offer for the whole company, but he made no predictions as to the timing of such an offer.
He did say in an interview with Reuters earlier this month that Hollinger was nearer making a move.

"I think he would like to grab the stock before any potential increase in the stock because of falling newsprint prices," said Ben Dube, a publishing analyst at Montreal-based Credifinance Securities.

Hollinger said it expected Southam, Canada's largest-circulation newspaper group, to set up a special committee of directors independent of Hollinger to consider the bid and make a recommendation to the board. The offer is expected to be mailed to Southam holders by Nov. 4.

Black's Southam purchase has raised hackles in Canada. Holding the reins of Southam as owner as well as chief executive in addition to his existing stable of newspapers gives Black effective control over nearly half the circulation in Canada.

A left-leaning public interest group called the Council of Canadians is asking a high Canadian court, the Federal Court of Canada, to quash the early approval Hollinger won for its purchase of the Southam shares from Power Corp.

David Robinson, research director of the organisation, said the group has asked for time to conclude research into what changes Hollinger has wrought in those Canadian newspapers it has so far purchased.

Since Hollinger took control, the Southam group has seen the resignation of two of its editors, a number of executives including Chief Executive William Ardell and several other editorial employees -- some citing differences of opinion with Black as their chief reason for departing.
Southam has also either sold or put on the block all its non-newspaper publishing assets. This week it also made deep cuts at its national advertising division, ADitus.
